scenes.dialogue: Your client is arrested. Police want him for questioning. Will it be police custody, or judicial custody? Who holds him, who authorises it, and for how long?
Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, or B N S S, these are distinct forms of detention, with safeguards.
scenes.shown: Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, or BNSS, these are distinct forms of detention, with safeguards.

scenes.dialogue: Here is the first deadline. After arrest without warrant, Section Fifty Eight prohibits detention beyond twenty four hours without a Magistrate's authorisation.
scenes.shown: Here is the first deadline. After arrest without warrant, Section 58 prohibits detention beyond 24 hours without a Magistrate's authorisation.

scenes.dialogue: Necessary travel time to court is excluded, and police must avoid unnecessary delay. Note the exact arrest time.
Ravi is arrested on Monday morning. Police cannot keep him at the station for days because questioning is unfinished.
If police need further detention, Section One Eighty Seven requires production before a Magistrate, who must consider whether remand is justified.
scenes.shown: If police need further detention, Section 187 requires production before a Magistrate, who must consider whether remand is justified.

scenes.dialogue: Who holds your client, and why? In police custody, he is entrusted to investigating police, for lawful investigation under the remand order.
That can include lawful questioning, or recovering evidence. Judicial custody is different: the accused is ordinarily kept in prison.
Jail authorities hold him, on the court's order. The investigating officer does not have the same direct custody.
Both forms require legal justification. Neither is a finding of guilt, and judicial custody does not mean a conviction.
Is it fifteen, or forty? Here is the key limit in the ordinary B N S S scheme.
scenes.shown: Is it 15, or 40? Here is the key limit in the ordinary BNSS scheme.

scenes.dialogue: Section One Eighty Seven, sub section Two, as the Supreme Court reads it, allows fifteen police custody days in all. Each grant still needs the Magistrate's decision.
scenes.shown: Section 187(2), as the Supreme Court reads it, allows 15 police-custody days in all. Each grant still needs the Magistrate's decision.

scenes.dialogue: Together or in parts, those days must all fall within the first forty days of remand in a sixty day case, or the first sixty in a ninety day case.
scenes.shown: Together or in parts, those days must all fall within the first 40 days of remand in a 60-day case, or the first 60 in a 90-day case.

scenes.dialogue: Forty and sixty only describe the window, not the number of days police may keep someone. The Supreme Court confirmed this in July twenty twenty six.
scenes.shown: Forty and sixty only describe the window, not the number of days police may keep someone. The Supreme Court confirmed this in July 2026.

scenes.dialogue: Test it on Ravi. Assume his case is in the sixty day category, and he stays in custody throughout. The Magistrate grants five days of police custody.
scenes.shown: Test it on Ravi. Assume his case is in the 60-day category, and he stays in custody throughout. The Magistrate grants five days of police custody.

scenes.dialogue: Then judicial custody follows. New evidence emerges, and on day twenty, the police ask for another five days.
scenes.shown: Then judicial custody follows. New evidence emerges, and on day 20, the police ask for another five days.

scenes.dialogue: Can the Magistrate grant them? Yes, if they are justified, because all five days fall within the first forty days, and only ten of the fifteen would be used.
scenes.shown: Can the Magistrate grant them? Yes, if they are justified, because all five days fall within the first 40 days, and only ten of the fifteen would be used.

scenes.dialogue: But returning to police custody does not create a fresh fifteen day allowance, or restart the overall remand clock. Check two numbers: days used, and the window.
scenes.shown: But returning to police custody does not create a fresh 15-day allowance, or restart the overall remand clock. Check two numbers: days used, and the window.

scenes.dialogue: Is a video link enough for police custody? No. Section One Eighty Seven, sub section Four, requires physical production before the Magistrate, each time.
scenes.shown: Is a video link enough for police custody? No. Section 187(4) requires physical production before the Magistrate, each time.

scenes.dialogue: For judicial custody, the rule is different: it may be extended through physical or audio video production.
scenes.shown: For judicial custody, the rule is different: it may be extended through physical or audio-video production.

scenes.dialogue: Under sub section Seven, the Magistrate must record reasons for police custody. A police request is not a remand order, so check the order for reasons.
scenes.shown: Under sub-section (7), the Magistrate must record reasons for police custody. A police request is not a remand order, so check the order for reasons.

scenes.dialogue: And to move Ravi from prison into police custody, investigators need a fresh court order, within the limits.
Where do sixty and ninety come from? Section One Eighty Seven, sub section Three, sets the investigation detention periods linked to default bail.
scenes.shown: Where do 60 and 90 come from? Section 187(3) sets the investigation detention periods linked to default bail.

scenes.dialogue: That is ninety days for offences punishable with death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment for ten years or more, and sixty days for other offences.
scenes.shown: That is 90 days for offences punishable with death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment for 10 years or more, and 60 days for other offences.

scenes.dialogue: Police and judicial custody both count towards that total. It is not fifteen days plus another sixty or ninety.
scenes.shown: Police and judicial custody both count towards that total. It is not 15 days plus another 60 or 90.

scenes.dialogue: Check the exact charge and the applicable judicial interpretation. Special laws can also modify these rules.
The period ends, and the required charge sheet is missing. Is your client free? Expiry alone does not open the prison gates.
Your client must claim default bail in time, and must be ready to furnish bail. A timely charge sheet can let judicial custody continue, through lawful orders.
After cognizance or the start of trial, Section Three Forty Six permits remand when proceedings are postponed or adjourned.
scenes.shown: After cognizance or the start of trial, Section 346 permits remand when proceedings are postponed or adjourned.

scenes.dialogue: That is at most fifteen days at a time under that section. Do not confuse it with the fifteen day police custody limit.
scenes.shown: That is at most 15 days at a time under that section. Do not confuse it with the 15-day police-custody limit.

scenes.dialogue: Custody does not remove basic rights. Section Forty Seven requires the grounds of arrest to be communicated forthwith.
scenes.shown: Custody does not remove basic rights. Section 47 requires the grounds of arrest to be communicated forthwith.

scenes.dialogue: Section Forty Eight requires that a nominated relative or friend be informed.
scenes.shown: Section 48 requires that a nominated relative or friend be informed.

scenes.dialogue: Section Thirty Eight gives your client the right to meet an advocate of his choice during interrogation, though not throughout it.
scenes.shown: Section 38 gives your client the right to meet an advocate of his choice during interrogation, though not throughout it.

scenes.dialogue: Sections Fifty Three and Fifty Six provide for medical examination, and for the arrested person's health and safety.
scenes.shown: Sections 53 and 56 provide for medical examination, and for the arrested person's health and safety.

scenes.dialogue: And bail can be sought before the maximum custody periods expire: the court need not use every available day.
Remember the two ordinary limits: twenty four hours before a Magistrate must authorise detention, and fifteen police custody days in all.
scenes.shown: Remember the two ordinary limits: 24 hours before a Magistrate must authorise detention, and 15 police-custody days in all.

scenes.dialogue: All of it sits inside the forty, sixty and ninety day framework. Count the days, check the order, and claim default bail in time.
scenes.shown: All of it sits inside the 40, 60 and 90-day framework. Count the days, check the order, and claim default bail in time.
